A stream key is a place inside the file, so the destination is the key alone and the path is named once, in FileBroker::new. Under size_limit, the publish that reaches the cap fails with SeaFileError::Publish, and every later publish to that file returns that error at once. A publisher kept from before the shutdown returns SeaFileError::NotConnected. A hook registered with after_startup runs once the subscriptions are open, and a hook that returns an error stops the startup.

The service leaves a record under lifecycle each time it starts. Macros Manual examples/file_publish.rs /// The record a service leaves in the file each time it starts. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "lifecycle")] struct Started { service: String, } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b // Runs once the subscriptions are open; a refused append fails the startup. .after_startup(Publish, async move |file| { file.message(&Started { service: "shipping".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }) .include(ship) }, ) } examples/manual/file_publish.rs /// The record a service leaves in the file each time it starts. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "lifecycle")] struct Started { service: String, } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b // Runs once the subscriptions are open; a refused append fails the startup. .after_startup(Publish, async move |file| { file.message(&Started { service: "shipping".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }) .include(subscriber("orders", Ship).build()) }, ) }

A stdio publish writes one line to standard output under its stream key; an empty message is refused because a pipe drops empty lines. StdioPublish, Publish in stdio::prelude, pairs into a StdioPublisher. A publish writes one line in the line format, with the message's stream key in its header. The next stage of the pipeline reads that line. This process's own subscriptions do not, because standard output never reaches the same process's standard input; loopback changes that for a test. A payload a text line would change, such as binary data or a payload with a newline, leaves in an envelope and arrives whole (Payloads). A message with no payload and no headers would be an empty line, which the line format drops. So the publisher refuses it with SeaFileError::Invalid, and nothing is written.

The stage answers each word with the same word in capitals, as a line under shouts. Macros Manual examples/stdio_publish.rs /// The line this stage writes for the next one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shouts")] struct Shout { text: String, } /// Answers each word with the same word in capitals. #[subscriber("words", reply)] async fn shout(word: &Word) -> Shout { Shout { text: word.text.to_uppercase(), } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shouter", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(shout).out_retry(Publish).to("words.retry") }) } examples/manual/stdio_publish.rs /// The line this stage writes for the next one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "shouts")] struct Shout { text: String, } /// Answers each word with the same word in capitals. struct ShoutBack; impl Handle<Word, Shout> for ShoutBack { fn handle( &self, word: &Word, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Shout, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Shout { text: word.text.to_uppercase(), })) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shouter", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("words", ShoutBack).reply().build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("words.retry") }) }

ack and nack report Unsupported on both brokers: nothing records how far a service read, so it resumes from a stored position. A handler settles a delivery as on any broker, with HandlerOutcome::ack or another outcome. The runtime passes the settlement to the transport, which answers AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning naming the subscription. A stream file keeps no record of a reader, and the file client's resumable mode is not implemented. So a subscription opens where its descriptor says on every start, whatever the previous run acknowledged. A service that resumes stores the sequence it reached, read with Ctx<Position>, and opens the next run there with start_at. A pipe has no log to go back to: a line read is gone, whatever the handler answers. What a handler asks for beyond ack still happens, because the runtime does it: retry_after on a stream file, out_retry on a pipe, a cap and a dead-letter key on both.

The service invoices every order the file holds; acknowledged orders are read again on the next start. Macros Manual examples/sea_acknowledgement.rs /// Invoices every order the file holds, on every start. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), start_at(FilePosition::beginning()))] async fn invoice(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); // Reported as unsupported: the next start reads this order again. HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The invoicing service on the file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| b.include(invoice)) } examples/manual/sea_acknowledgement.rs /// Invoices every order the file holds, on every start. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); // Reported as unsupported: the next start reads this order again. ready(Ok(())) } } /// The invoicing service on the file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Invoice) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ) }) }

dead_letter names the stream key a spent delivery is written to, with its payload, its headers and its delivery count. dead_letter(key) goes beside max_attempts(n). The delivery that reaches the cap is published under that key instead of coming back. It keeps its payload and the headers it arrived with, and its retry count says how many deliveries the message got. On a stream file the key is one more stream inside the same file. On a pipe it is a line under that key, which a downstream stage reads. A service reads the dead letters with a subscription of their own, or a replay when an operator inspects them.

A label that fails three times is written under labels.dead. Macros Manual examples/file_dead_letter.rs /// Prints a parcel label; the printer is jammed, so every attempt asks for another. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("labels"))] async fn print(label: &Label) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(label.parcel, "printer jammed"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("labels", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/labels.ss"), |b| { b.include(print) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("labels.dead") }, ) } examples/manual/file_dead_letter.rs /// Prints a parcel label; the printer is jammed, so every attempt asks for another. struct Print; impl Handle<Label> for Print { fn handle( &self, label: &Label, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(label.parcel, "printer jammed"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY))) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("labels", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/labels.ss"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("labels"), Print).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("labels.dead") }, ) }

On a pipe a deferred copy goes to the next stage, so the mount site names it with out_retry(Publish).to(key) or the service does not start. out_retry(policy) names the publisher the runtime's deferred copies leave through, and .to(key) names the stream key they go to. Standard output reaches the next process in the pipeline and never this one's standard input. So a copy cannot come back to the stage that deferred it, and the stage says where it goes. Every registration on StdioBroker names it, because a handler may answer retry_after on any delivery. A registration that names none stops the service at startup, with an error that names the subscription and the .to(..) step that fixes it. The copy leaves once the delay is over, and a downstream stage reads it under that key, for example to feed it back to the start of the pipeline. On a stream file the copy needs no destination (retry_after), and out_retry(Publish) there only replaces the publisher. The position is a slot, so .transform(..) runs on the copy; the copy carries the delivery's own bytes, so no codec encodes it.

The stage hands every job it cannot run now to jobs.retry after five seconds. Macros Manual examples/stdio_out_retry.rs /// Hands every job it cannot run now to the retry stage, after a pause. #[subscriber("jobs")] async fn work(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "busy, deferring"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(work).out_retry(Publish).to("jobs.retry") }) } examples/manual/stdio_out_retry.rs /// Hands every job it cannot run now to the retry stage, after a pause. struct Work; impl Handle<Job> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "busy, deferring"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY))) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("jobs.retry") }) }

max_attempts caps how many deliveries a message gets, counted in the framework's retry-count header that every copy carries. max_attempts(n) follows include at the mount site; n counts the first delivery too. Neither transport counts redeliveries, so the count is RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, which the runtime writes on every copy. A handler reads the header off its context to know which attempt it runs. Under a cap, an immediate retry travels as a copy too, because the count lives in the header. The delivery that reaches the cap is rejected and no copy follows it. A cap with no dead-letter key beside it writes the spent delivery nowhere. A registration mounted by a bare stream key takes the cap the same way as one mounted by a FileStream. The guide Retries and dead letters caps a service's retries on a stream file and on a pipe.

The printer is jammed, so every attempt asks for another; the third delivery is the last. Macros Manual examples/file_max_attempts.rs /// Prints a parcel label; the printer is jammed, so every attempt asks for another. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("labels"))] async fn print(label: &Label, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let attempt = ctx .headers() .get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| count.parse::<u32>().ok()) .unwrap_or(0); tracing::info!(label.parcel, attempt, "printer jammed"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("labels", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/labels.ss"), |b| { b.include(print).max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) }) } examples/manual/file_max_attempts.rs /// Prints a parcel label; the printer is jammed, so every attempt asks for another. struct Print; impl Handle<Label> for Print { fn handle( &self, label: &Label, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let attempt = ctx .headers() .get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| count.parse::<u32>().ok()) .unwrap_or(0); tracing::info!(label.parcel, attempt, "printer jammed"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY))) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("labels", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/labels.ss"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("labels"), Print).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) }, ) }

On a stream file a retry_after copy is appended under the key the subscription reads, so it comes back with nothing named at the mount site. retry_after(delay) asks for a later delivery. A stream file cannot hold a message back, so the runtime does it. It settles the delivery, waits out the delay and publishes a copy of the message, payload and headers, through the form's Publish. One stream key is both ends of the file, so the copy is appended under the key the subscription reads, and the subscription reads it as the next message. This holds for a FileStream and for a bare stream key alike. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER incremented, and the handler reads it like any other header. The copy waits in the service's memory, so a process that exits before the delay is over loses it. A replay reads the copy while the replay is still short of the end of the file, and leaves it unread once it has passed that point. out_retry replaces the publisher the copy leaves through, and a transform on that position runs on the copy.

The first attempt finds the card processor busy; the copy comes back 30 seconds later and is charged. Macros Manual examples/file_retry_after.rs /// Charges a payment; the first attempt finds the card processor busy and asks again later. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("payments"))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { // A copy carries the framework's retry count; the first delivery carries none. if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(payment.id, "processor busy, trying later"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "charged"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/payments.ss"), |b| { b.include(charge) }) } examples/manual/file_retry_after.rs /// Charges a payment; the first attempt finds the card processor busy and asks again later. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { // A copy carries the framework's retry count; the first delivery carries none. if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(payment.id, "processor busy, trying later"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY))); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "charged"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/payments.ss"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("payments"), Charge).build()) }) }

A stream key in #[subscriber] is a subscription on both brokers; on a stream file it follows the live tail of that key. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the stream key orders. A stream file holds many keys side by side, and a line on a pipe names its key in its header, so on both brokers the key is the whole subscription. On a stream file the subscription opens at the tip and reads every message appended under its key from then on. What the file held before the service started is read from a position or in a replay. A key is 1 to 249 characters of ASCII letters, digits, ., _ and -; a subscription to any other key stops the service at startup with an error that names the key. On a stream file, the descriptor FileStream opens the same subscription and adds the replay mode and a channel description in the generated document. On a pipe the key is the only form, and Lines shows how a line names it. The manual form passes the key to subscriber(name, body).

Every order appended under orders while the service runs is shipped. Macros Manual examples/file_subscriptions.rs /// Ships every order appended under the `orders` key while the service runs. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "shipping"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(ship) }) } examples/manual/file_subscriptions.rs /// Ships every order appended under the `orders` key while the service runs. struct Ship; impl Handle<Order> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "shipping"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Ship).build()) }) }

A slice handler takes a batch assembled on the client, up to the size batch(n) names; a partial batch leaves 10 ms after its first delivery. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. Both clients read one message at a time, so the crate assembles each batch on the client, on a stream file and on a pipe alike. A batch takes what the transport already holds, up to n, and does not wait to fill up. A batch that is not full goes out 10 ms after its first delivery, so at a quiet tail a batch is often one message. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles message i with outcome i, and a single HandlerOutcome settles the whole batch. A batch body on a stream file reaches the seek handle through FileBatchContext. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) settles the whole batch and Err(outcomes) settles message by message.

The handler sums a batch of readings and settles each one. Macros Manual examples/file_batches.rs /// Sums a batch of readings and settles each one; a batch is at most the size the mount site /// names, and smaller when the file had no more. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("readings"), start_at(FilePosition::beginning()))] async fn aggregate(batch: &[Reading]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { let total: u32 = batch.iter().map(|reading| reading.millivolts).sum(); tracing::info!(readings = batch.len(), total, "aggregated"); batch.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::ack()).collect() } examples/manual/file_batches.rs /// Sums a batch of readings; `Ok` settles the whole batch. struct Aggregate; impl Handle<[Reading]> for Aggregate { fn handle( &self, batch: &[Reading], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let total: u32 = batch.iter().map(|reading| reading.millivolts).sum(); tracing::info!(readings = batch.len(), total, "aggregated"); ready(Ok(())) } }

Ten readings recorded in the file arrive as batches of four, four and two. Macros Manual examples/file_batches.rs /// The service on the sensors' stream file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("readings", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(file, |b| b.include(aggregate.batch(nonzero!(4)))) } examples/manual/file_batches.rs /// The service on the sensors' stream file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("readings", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("readings"), Aggregate) .batch(nonzero!(4)) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ) }) }

FileStream names one stream key of the file and is the descriptor the generated document describes. FileStream::new(key) goes where a stream key goes, as the first argument of #[subscriber]. It reads what the bare key reads: the messages appended under that key once the service has started. The file itself is named once, by FileBroker::new(path), so every descriptor of a service reads the same file. Where reading begins is a position, set with start_at. The descriptor adds two things to the bare key. replay() reads the retained file once and completes, a reading mode a position cannot express. Under the asyncapi feature the subscription's channel carries its stream key in the x-ruststream-file extension of the generated document, as Channels shows; a bare key describes nothing there. A retry_after copy is appended under the descriptor's key, so it comes back to the same subscription with nothing named at the mount site (retry_after). An empty key or a key the file does not take stops the service at startup. The manual form passes the descriptor to subscriber(..) where a key would go.

Two orders were in the file when the service started; the service ships the third, the first appended after it. Macros Manual examples/file_stream.rs /// Ships the orders appended under the `orders` key after the service started. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"))] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "shipping"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The service on the stream file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| b.include(ship)) } examples/manual/file_stream.rs /// Ships the orders appended under the `orders` key after the service started. struct Ship; impl Handle<Order> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "shipping"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The service on the stream file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Ship).build()) }) }

A stdio subscription reads the lines of its stream key; a line with no key in its header reaches every subscription. #[subscriber("jobs")] on StdioBroker reads the lines of standard input whose header names the key jobs. A line is a header in square brackets, then the payload: [timestamp | stream_key | sequence | shard_id] payload. Every field of the header is optional, so [jobs] {"id":7} names the key alone. A line under another key is passed over, so a stage takes the keys it subscribed to out of a shared stream. A line with no header names no key, and the client hands it to every subscription of the stage, whatever key the subscription reads. The stage parses each header before the service sees the line. A line it cannot read is passed over with a warning in the log: input that is not UTF-8, or a leading [...] that is not a header, a JSON array among them. So a producer writes a header in front of a payload that opens with [. A stdio subscription reads lines as they arrive, and ends when standard input ends, after the lines it has already read. A delivery reports the sequence its header names, or the count of its key's lines from zero when the header names none. A reply is a line on standard output under the key its type declares, and the next stage reads it. Every registration on a pipe names where a deferred copy goes, with out_retry(Publish).to(key).

The stage answers each jobs line with a results line for the next stage. Macros Manual examples/stdio_lines.rs /// Answers each `jobs` line with a `results` line for the next stage. #[subscriber("jobs", reply)] async fn work(job: &Job) -> Done { Done { id: job.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(work).out_retry(Publish).to("jobs.retry") }) } examples/manual/stdio_lines.rs /// Answers each `jobs` line with a `results` line for the next stage. struct Work; impl Handle<Job, Done> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Done, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Done { id: job.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).reply().build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("jobs.retry") }) }

replay reads the whole retained file once and completes at its end or at the end-of-stream mark, instead of following writes. FileStream::new("orders").replay() turns the subscription into one pass over what the file holds under its key. It starts at the first message the file retains and delivers every message in order. It completes at the end of the file, or at the end-of-stream mark a writer left with end_with_eos, and a message appended after that point is not read. That suits a job over a finished log: an audit, a migration, an index rebuilt from scratch. start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) on a plain descriptor reads the same messages and then goes on following new writes. A seek from a handler still moves a replay, one that has reached the end included, and the replay goes on from the new position (Seek). A seek to a position past the tip is refused, and the replay stays where it was. A retry_after copy reaches a replay while the replay is still short of the end, and is left unread once the replay has passed it. A service that only reads a finished file opens it with existing_only, so a wrong path stops it at startup instead of creating an empty file. The guide An event log on disk totals a finished file with a replay.

The audit reads the three orders of a finished day and completes; an order appended later is not read. Macros Manual examples/file_replay.rs /// Audits a finished day of orders in one pass. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders").replay())] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The audit of the day's file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| b.include(audit)) } fn main() -> ExitCode { // The shop wrote the day's file; the audit reads it and never creates one. run_main(|| app(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/2026-10-17.ss").existing_only())) } examples/manual/file_replay.rs /// Audits a finished day of orders in one pass. struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The audit of the day's file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("orders").replay(), Audit).build()) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { // The shop wrote the day's file; the audit reads it and never creates one. run_main(|| app(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/2026-10-17.ss").existing_only())) }

TestApp::start connects FileBroker to a log in memory and StdioBroker to a pipe in memory, with the production app unchanged. A test hands the harness the app main runs and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<FileBroker>() or tb.broker::<StdioBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode. No file is opened and no pipe is attached, so tests run side by side in one process. A stream file in process is a log in memory, new and empty for each broker value and shared by the broker's clones. It keeps what the file keeps: each stream key numbered from one, a live subscription that starts at the tip, a replay that completes at the end of the log, positions and seeking with the file's refusals, and the end-of-stream mark. A test publishes into the log, and published::<T>(key) reads what the service appended, retry copies and dead letters included. A pipe in process is standard input the test feeds and standard output the service writes. A message the test publishes is a line arriving under its key. A line the service writes is recorded under its key, and published::<T>(key) reads it the way the next stage would. It reaches the service's own subscriptions only under loopback, as on a real pipe. Both refuse what the real transport refuses: a stream key the client does not take, an empty line on a pipe, a beacon interval that is not a multiple of 1024. A header crosses the same envelope a file or a line carries. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, so the assertions read finished state; tb.advance(..) on a paused clock brings a retry_after copy back. What only the real transport shows, such as the bytes of a .ss file or what a file keeps across runs, is for a live test. The guide Testing a file or pipeline service tests a whole service this way.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-sea-file = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } A file service answers an order with a receipt. Macros Manual examples/sea_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { order: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/sea_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { order: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } A pipeline stage answers a jobs line with a results line, which the test reads off the stage's standard output. Macros Manual examples/sea_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_job_line_gets_a_result_line() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(stage()).await?; // A line on the stage's standard input. tb.broker::<StdioBroker>() .message(&Job { id: 7 }) .to("jobs") .publish() .await?; // A line the stage wrote to its standard output. tb.broker::<StdioBroker>() .published::<Done>("results") .assert_called_once() .with(&Done { job: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/sea_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_job_line_gets_a_result_line() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(stage()).await?; // A line on the stage's standard input. tb.broker::<StdioBroker>() .message(&Job { id: 7 }) .to("jobs") .publish() .await?; // A line the stage wrote to its standard output. tb.broker::<StdioBroker>() .published::<Done>("results") .assert_called_once() .with(&Done { job: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) }

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a real stream file in a temp directory; no server is needed. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so the file is created, written and read by the file client. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it, ten seconds at most. start_live_within sets another bound. The file is the whole stand, so a live test runs on any machine, in the same cargo test as the rest. Each run takes a path of its own, so nothing an earlier run appended is read, and removes the file at the end. The live mode is for what the log in memory leaves out: the bytes of a .ss file, what a file keeps across two runs of a service, and a file that existing_only refuses. Two runs on one path show a service resuming at a stored position, or reading again what it acknowledged. A stdio stage is tested live as a child process with piped standard input and output, because a stdio broker in a test process would take that process's own pipes.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one on a stream file of the run's own. Macros Manual examples/file_testing_live.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn confirms_an_order(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { order: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { confirms_an_order(TestApp::start(app("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss")).await?).await } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn on_a_stream_file() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // A file of this run's own, so nothing an earlier run appended is read. let path = env::temp_dir().join(format!("ruststream-sea-file-live-{}.ss", process::id())); let path = path.to_string_lossy().into_owned(); confirms_an_order(TestApp::start_live(app(&path)).await?).await?; fs::remove_file(&path)?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/file_testing_live.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn confirms_an_order(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { order: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { confirms_an_order(TestApp::start(app("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss")).await?).await } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn on_a_stream_file() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // A file of this run's own, so nothing an earlier run appended is read. let path = env::temp_dir().join(format!("ruststream-sea-file-live-{}.ss", process::id())); let path = path.to_string_lossy().into_owned(); confirms_an_order(TestApp::start_live(app(&path)).await?).await?; fs::remove_file(&path)?; Ok(()) }

This guide records a shop's events in a stream file, follows them as they are written and totals a finished file in one pass. A stream file is a log: a publish appends a message under a stream key, and every reader of the key sees it in order. The example is a shop that records a receipt for each order, and an audit job that totals the receipts of a finished file.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, /// Where the order sits under `orders`, so a reader can move back to it. sequence: u64, } /// Records a receipt for each order, appended to the same file under `receipts`. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), reply)] async fn checkout(order: &Order, Ctx(at): Ctx<Position>) -> Receipt { let sequence = match at { FilePosition::Sequence(sequence) => sequence, // A delivery always sits at a sequence; the other forms name places to start from. FilePosition::Beginning | FilePosition::End | FilePosition::Timestamp(_) => 0, }; Receipt { order: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, sequence, } } /// Follows the receipts as the shop writes them. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("receipts"))] async fn notify(receipt: &Receipt) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(receipt.order, "customer notified"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn shop(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(file, |b| b.include(checkout).include(notify)) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(|| shop(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"))) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Receipt { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, /// Where the order sits under `orders`, so a reader can move back to it. sequence: u64, } /// Records a receipt for each order, appended to the same file under `receipts`. struct Checkout; impl Handle<Order, Receipt, (), FileContext> for Checkout { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { let sequence = match ctx.context(Position) { FilePosition::Sequence(sequence) => sequence, // A delivery always sits at a sequence; the other forms name places to start from. FilePosition::Beginning | FilePosition::End | FilePosition::Timestamp(_) => 0, }; ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, sequence, })) } } /// Follows the receipts as the shop writes them. struct Notify; impl Handle<Receipt> for Notify { fn handle( &self, receipt: &Receipt, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(receipt.order, "customer notified"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn shop(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Checkout) .reply() .build(), ) .include(subscriber(FileStream::new("receipts"), Notify).build()) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(|| shop(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"))) } checkout answers each order with a Receipt, and the reply is appended to the same file under receipts, the key the type declares. One file holds every stream key, so the path is named once, in FileBroker::new. A publish appends the message and flushes it, so the bytes reach the operating system before the call returns. The file is synced to the device when the broker shuts down. notify follows receipts from the end of the file and reads each receipt as checkout appends it. Another process that opens the same path follows the key the same way. A subscription with no position starts at the end, so a restarted notify reads only the receipts written after it started. Each stream key is numbered from one. The receipt keeps the order's sequence, which Ctx<Position> hands the handler, so a reader can move back to that order later. A later run that appends to the same file carries the numbering on: after a restart the next order is number three, not one. The file grows without limit, unless size_limit caps it. Running in production covers what a cap means for a long-lived file.

Macros Manual src/bin/audit.rs /// Totals the receipts of a finished file, up to 64 at a time; one outcome settles the batch. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("receipts").replay())] async fn total(batch: &[Receipt]) -> HandlerOutcome { let cents: u64 = batch.iter().map(|receipt| receipt.amount_cents).sum(); tracing::info!(receipts = batch.len(), cents, "receipts totalled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The audit job: it reads the shop's file and never creates one. fn audit(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file.existing_only(), |b| { b.include(total.batch(nonzero!(64))) }) } src/bin/audit.rs /// Totals the receipts of a finished file, up to 64 at a time; `Ok` settles the whole batch. struct Total; impl Handle<[Receipt]> for Total { fn handle( &self, batch: &[Receipt], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let cents: u64 = batch.iter().map(|receipt| receipt.amount_cents).sum(); tracing::info!(receipts = batch.len(), cents, "receipts totalled"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The audit job: it reads the shop's file and never creates one. fn audit(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file.existing_only(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("receipts").replay(), Total) .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ) }) } replay() reads what the file holds under receipts from the first message and completes at the end of the file. A receipt appended after that point is not read, so the job does its pass and has nothing more to wait for. existing_only makes startup fail when the file is missing, so a mistyped path stops the job instead of creating an empty file. total takes a slice, and batch(nonzero!(64)) at the mount site caps a batch at 64 receipts. A batch takes what the file already holds and does not wait to fill up; one outcome settles the whole batch. A writer marks a file finished with end_with_eos, which appends an end-of-stream mark at shutdown. A replay completes at the mark, and a live subscription such as notify ends on it.

The tests in the example file run the shop and the audit in process: an order gets its receipt and notify reads it, and the audit reads three recorded receipts in one batch and ignores a fourth. The audit's receipts are recorded on a clone of its broker before it starts, the way the shop would have left them. The restart test runs the shop twice on one real file with TestApp::start_live and checks that the second run numbers its order three. Testing a file or pipeline service covers both modes.
This guide installs ruststream-sea-file, runs a first service on a stream file and moves the same handler into a shell pipeline. Neither transport needs a server.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.8", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-sea-file = "0.8" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-sea-file = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-sea-file holds both transports. Its testing feature adds the in-process transports that tests run on, and asyncapi adds what the crate contributes to the AsyncAPI document. Both features are off by default. The stream file client builds on Unix systems only, so the crate does not build on Windows.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_sea_file::file::prelude::*; use serde::Deserialize; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), start_at(FilePosition::beginning()))] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(FileBroker::new("/tmp/orders.ss"), |b| b.include(take_order)) } src/main.rs use ruststream_sea_file::file::prelude::*; use serde::Deserialize; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/tmp/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), TakeOrder) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders under the stream key orders of the file /tmp/orders.ss. It acknowledges an order with an amount and drops one without. FileBroker::new only records the path. The file opens when the service starts, and startup creates it when it is missing. FileStream::new names the stream key, and start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) reads the key from the start of the file instead of from its end. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run It reads every order the file holds, then waits for the next one. Another service appends an order by publishing it under orders on the same path, as An event log on disk shows. Ctrl+C stops the service.

The file client ships a decoder that prints a stream file one message per line: cargo install sea-streamer-file --features=executables --bin ss-decode ss-decode --file /tmp/orders.ss Each line is [timestamp | stream key | sequence | shard] payload, for example [2026-10-18T09:12:03.120 | orders | 1 | 0] {"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}. One file holds every stream key, and each key is numbered from one. A new file also holds one message under the key ruststream-internal, which the crate writes when it creates the file.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. FileBroker runs in process there, so the tests touch no file: cargo test Testing a file or pipeline service walks through the harness and what the in-process transports model.

The other transport reads standard input and writes standard output. The handler stays as it is; the prelude, the broker and the subscription change. Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_sea_file::stdio::prelude::*; use serde::Deserialize; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(take_order).out_retry(Publish).to("orders.retry") }) } src/main.rs use ruststream_sea_file::stdio::prelude::*; use serde::Deserialize; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", TakeOrder).build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("orders.retry") }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } StdioBroker::new takes no settings, and the subscription names the stream key alone. A stage names the key its deferred copies go to with out_retry(Publish).to(..), and it does not start without one. The publish policy is called Publish in both preludes, so code that publishes reads the same on either transport. Feed the stage a line: echo '[orders] {"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' | cargo run -- run The square brackets name the stream key. The log goes to standard error, because standard output carries the stage's messages to the next process. Shell pipelines covers the line format and chained stages.

documents.t: A service on sea-streamer-file writes its own consumer loop and producer. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: sea-streamer RustStream FileStreamer::connect with FileConnectOptions FileBroker::new and its settings, applied at startup create_consumer and a next() loop a #[subscriber] handler on a FileStream decoding the message payload the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec create_producer and send_to a reply or an Out parameter, sent through Publish set_auto_stream_reset on the consumer options, then seek_to start_at at the mount site, or the seek handle in the handler (Resuming and seeking) StdioStreamer StdioBroker

This guide runs a service as one stage of a shell pipeline, producer | stage | consumer. StdioBroker reads the process's standard input as a stream and writes its standard output. A subscription reads the lines of one stream key, and a publish writes a line for the next process. The example is a pricing stage: it reads orders and answers each one with a receipt.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream::runtime::RustStreamError; use ruststream_sea_file::stdio::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, quantity: u64, unit_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, total_cents: u64, } #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn price(order: &Order) -> Receipt { let total_cents = order.quantity * order.unit_cents; // The log goes to standard error; standard output carries only messages. tracing::info!(order.id, total_cents, "order priced"); Receipt { order: order.id, total_cents, } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("pricing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b // A deferred copy leaves on standard output under this key, for a later stage. .include(price) .out_retry(Publish) .to("orders.retry") }) } src/main.rs use ruststream_sea_file::stdio::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, quantity: u64, unit_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Receipt { order: u64, total_cents: u64, } struct Price; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Price { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { let total_cents = order.quantity * order.unit_cents; // The log goes to standard error; standard output carries only messages. tracing::info!(order.id, total_cents, "order priced"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id, total_cents, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("pricing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b // A deferred copy leaves on standard output under this key, for a later stage. .include(subscriber("orders", Price).reply().build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("orders.retry") }) } price reads the lines under orders and replies with a Receipt, which leaves on standard output under receipts. The stage needs out_retry(Publish).to(..) even though price never retries: on a pipe a deferred copy can only go to a later stage, so every registration names the key, and the stage does not start without it.

A line is a header in square brackets, then the payload (Lines): [timestamp | stream_key | sequence | shard_id] payload Every field of the header is optional, so a producer usually writes the key alone: echo '[orders] {"id":7,"quantity":3,"unit_cents":250}' | ./pricing A line under another key is passed over, so several stages can take their own keys out of one stream. A line with no header names no key, and the client hands it to every subscription of the stage. So a tool that writes plain JSON lines feeds every handler at once: jq -c '.[]' orders.json | ./pricing The stage parses the header of each line before the service sees it. A line it cannot read is passed over with a warning in the log, and the stage reads on. Two kinds of line are passed over: input that is not UTF-8, and a leading [...] that is not a header, such as a JSON array. A producer of such payloads writes a header in front of each one.

The stage writes one line per publish, with a header the client fills in: [2026-10-18T15:08:01 | receipts | 0] {"order":7,"total_cents":750} The timestamp is the time of writing, to the second, and the sequence counts each key's lines from zero. A tool that reads plain JSON takes the payload after the header: ./pricing < orders.txt | sed 's/^\[[^]]*\] //' | jq .total_cents A payload that a text line would change leaves in an envelope: a binary payload, one with a newline or padding, and every message with headers. An envelope is a line starting with rs1: or rs2:, meant for the next RustStream stage, which opens it and hands its handler the bytes and headers that were published. The log goes to standard error through tracing, so it never mixes with the messages. A line printed to standard output with println! reaches the next stage as a line with no key, and every subscription there reads it.

src/main.rs /// Runs the stage until its input ends: the end of standard input ends the subscription, and /// the stage then shuts down and exits. #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), RustStreamError> { let running = app().start().await?; let mut health = running.health(); while health.is_running() && health.subscriptions().active > 0 { health.changed().await; } running.shutdown().await } When standard input ends, every subscription of the stage ends after the lines it has already read. main starts the service and watches the HealthProbe, which counts the subscriptions that still read. When none is left, shutdown stops the service, and the stage exits with status 0. A fail-fast failure ends the wait too, and shutdown returns it as the error, so the stage exits with a failure status. So ./pricing < orders.txt prices every order in the file and exits. #[ruststream::app] runs the service until SIGINT or SIGTERM instead. That fits a stage that waits for input as long as it runs, such as one behind tail -f.

./intake < orders.txt | ./pricing | ./billing Each stage reads the keys it subscribes to and writes its replies for the next one. Headers and binary payloads cross every pipe whole, because each stage opens the envelopes the previous one wrote. A stage that retries later sends its copies down the pipe under the key its mount site names, and a later stage reads them, as Retries and dead letters shows.

The example file tests the stage in process: TestApp::start runs it, tb.broker::<StdioBroker>().message(..) injects an order line, and published::<Receipt>("receipts") reads the line it wrote. The live tests spawn the built stage with piped standard input and output. They check that it answers orders lines and lines with no key, passes over another key, a JSON array line and input that is not UTF-8, and exits when its input ends. loopback feeds a stage its own output, so two stages run in one process and one test drives both.
A stream file is the service's own storage, so the facts a networked broker keeps on its servers are the service's here: where the file lives, when its bytes reach the device and how large it grows.

src/main.rs /// The shop's stream file, at the path the deployment names. fn broker() -> FileBroker { let path = env::var("ORDERS_FILE").unwrap_or_else(|_| "/var/lib/shop/orders.ss".to_owned()); // A beacon every 256 KiB: a seek reads at most that far from the nearest one. FileBroker::new(path).beacon_interval(256 * 1024) } The deployment names the path in an environment variable. Startup creates the file when it is missing. A service that only reads a file another process writes opens it with existing_only, so a wrong path stops it at startup. beacon_interval sets how far apart the file's index entries sit. A seek reads forward from the nearest beacon, so closer beacons seek in finer steps and take more room; the client's default is one every 1 MiB. The interval must be a positive multiple of 1024, and any other value stops the service at startup. The file client builds on Unix systems only.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), reply)] async fn checkout(order: &Order) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Receipt { order: order.id } } fn service(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| b.include(checkout)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker()) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } struct Checkout; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Checkout { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id })) } } fn service(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Checkout) .reply() .build(), ) }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker()) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } app builds the service on the production broker, and the tests start that same app.

A publish appends the message under its stream key and flushes it, so the bytes reach the operating system before the call returns. A live reader in this process or another one sees the message from then on. The file is synced to the device when the broker shuts down. Between those points the operating system decides when the bytes reach the device. The file grows without limit, so the disk it lives on is the limit. size_limit sets a cap of its own. A publish that reaches the cap fails with SeaFileError::Publish, and so does every later publish to that file. A long-lived capped log therefore moves to a new file before it reaches the cap: the service starts on a new path, and readers of the old file finish it with a replay.

The broker's shutdown waits for the publishes in flight, writes the end-of-stream mark when the broker asks for one, and syncs the file. When shutdown returns the file is closed, so an after_shutdown hook can move or copy it. end_with_eos suits a writer whose file is complete when it stops, such as a daily log: a replay completes at the mark, and a live reader ends on it. A publisher kept from before the shutdown returns SeaFileError::NotConnected and never writes to the closed file.

A stage's standard output carries its messages, so its log goes to standard error through tracing. A line on standard output from anywhere else in the process reaches the next stage as a message. The stdio transport belongs to the whole process: shutting a StdioBroker down ends every stdio subscription and publisher in it.

Under the asyncapi feature the file broker is a server of the generated document with the protocol file, and its description is the path of the stream file. The document is shared with the people who read it, so the path is too.

The tests start the production app under TestApp::start, so the settings are checked the way startup checks them, without a file. A beacon interval that is not a multiple of 1024 fails the start in the test as it does on a real file.

This guide makes a service resume where its last run stopped, and moves a running subscription to another place in the file. A stream file keeps no record of how far a reader got. ack and nack report Unsupported on this transport (Acknowledgement), so a restarted subscription opens wherever its mount site says. A service that must not handle an order twice stores its own checkpoint. The example is an invoicing service that reads the shop's orders and invoices each one once, across restarts.

Macros Manual src/checkpoint.rs /// The sequence of the last order the service invoiced, kept in a file of its own. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] struct Checkpoint { path: Arc<Path>, } impl Checkpoint { fn new(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Self { Self { path: path.as_ref().into(), } } /// The stored sequence; `None` until the first order is invoiced. fn load(&self) -> Option<u64> { fs::read_to_string(&self.path).ok()?.trim().parse().ok() } fn store(&self, sequence: u64) -> io::Result<()> { fs::write(&self.path, sequence.to_string()) } } /// The app's state: each field reaches a handler as `State<FieldType>`. #[derive(Debug, Clone, FromRef)] struct Invoicing { checkpoint: Checkpoint, } src/checkpoint.rs /// The sequence of the last order the service invoiced, kept in a file of its own. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] struct Checkpoint { path: Arc<Path>, } impl Checkpoint { fn new(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Self { Self { path: path.as_ref().into(), } } /// The stored sequence; `None` until the first order is invoiced. fn load(&self) -> Option<u64> { fs::read_to_string(&self.path).ok()?.trim().parse().ok() } fn store(&self, sequence: u64) -> io::Result<()> { fs::write(&self.path, sequence.to_string()) } } #[derive(Debug, Clone)] struct Invoicing { checkpoint: Checkpoint, } The checkpoint is the sequence of the last order the service invoiced, in a file of its own. Invoicing is the app's state, and the handler takes the checkpoint from it. Any store the service already has works the same way: a database row, a key in a cache.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"))] async fn invoice( order: &Order, Ctx(at): Ctx<Position>, State(checkpoint): State<Checkpoint>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let FilePosition::Sequence(sequence) = at else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; // The run opens at the stored sequence, so the order the last run ended on comes again. if checkpoint.load().is_some_and(|stored| sequence <= stored) { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, sequence, "invoiced"); if let Err(error) = checkpoint.store(sequence) { tracing::error!(order.id, sequence, %error, "checkpoint not stored"); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn invoicing(file: FileBroker, checkpoint: Checkpoint) -> impl App<State = Invoicing> { let start = checkpoint .load() .map_or(FilePosition::beginning(), FilePosition::sequence); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Invoicing { checkpoint })) .with_broker(file, |b| b.include(invoice.start_at(start))) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(|| { invoicing( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), Checkpoint::new("/var/lib/shop/invoicing.checkpoint"), ) }) } src/main.rs struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order, (), (), FileContext, Invoicing> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileContext, Invoicing>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let FilePosition::Sequence(sequence) = ctx.context(Position) else { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); }; let checkpoint = &ctx.state().checkpoint; // The run opens at the stored sequence, so the order the last run ended on comes again. if checkpoint.load().is_some_and(|stored| sequence <= stored) { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, sequence, "invoiced"); if let Err(error) = checkpoint.store(sequence) { tracing::error!(order.id, sequence, %error, "checkpoint not stored"); } ready(Ok(())) } } fn invoicing(file: FileBroker, checkpoint: Checkpoint) -> impl App<State = Invoicing> { let start = checkpoint .load() .map_or(FilePosition::beginning(), FilePosition::sequence); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Invoicing { checkpoint })) .with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Invoice) .start_at(start) .build(), ) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(|| { invoicing( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), Checkpoint::new("/var/lib/shop/invoicing.checkpoint"), ) }) } invoicing reads the checkpoint before the service starts and passes it to start_at at the mount site. The first run has no checkpoint and reads the file from the beginning. FilePosition::sequence(n) delivers message n itself, so a run opened at the stored sequence gets the order the last run ended on once more. invoice reads the delivery's sequence with Ctx<Position> and drops an order at or below the checkpoint. Every other order is invoiced, and its sequence becomes the new checkpoint. The checkpoint is written after the invoice. A run that stops between the two invoices that order again on the next start, so the invoice itself must tolerate a repeat. Writing the checkpoint first gives the opposite trade: an order is never invoiced twice, and one can be lost. FilePosition::timestamp(ms) opens at the first message written after a moment, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. It suits a service that rebuilds its view from a point in time instead of from a stored sequence.

A handler moves its own subscription with Ctx<SeekHandle>. seek(FilePosition::end()) skips the backlog and goes on from the tip; seek(FilePosition::sequence(n)) goes back to message n or forward past a run of messages known to fail. The deliveries already queued from the old place are discarded, and the next delivery comes from the new one. A seek to a sequence past the next one the file writes is refused with an error: a live subscription then ends, and a replay stays where it was. A batch handler reaches the same handle through FileBatchContext.

The in-process tests record five orders before the service starts and store a checkpoint of three. The service reads orders three to five, drops the third and invoices the other two. The restart test runs the service twice on one real file with TestApp::start_live: the second run opens at the order the first one ended on and drops it. Testing a file or pipeline service covers both modes.

This guide retries a message later, caps its deliveries and moves what keeps failing to a dead-letter key. Neither transport holds a message back or counts its deliveries. The framework does both: a later delivery is a copy the runtime publishes once a delay has passed, and the count travels in a header of that copy. The example is a shipping service that ships an order once its payment has cleared.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long an order waits before the service asks the payment service again. const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, } #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, State(payments): State<Arc<Payments>>) -> HandlerOutcome { if !payments.has_cleared(order.id) { // The payment may clear later: ask again after a pause. return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// How long an order waits before the service asks the payment service again. const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, } struct Ship; impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), Clients> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !ctx.state().payments.has_cleared(order.id) { // The payment may clear later: ask again after a pause. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } Payments is the service's client of the payment service, kept in the app's state. While an order's payment has not cleared, ship answers retry_after and the service asks again two seconds later. retry_after settles the delivery, waits out the delay and appends a copy of the order under the key the subscription reads. The subscription reads the copy as a new message, after everything that was already in the file. So the orders behind a waiting one are not held up. The copy carries the retry-count header (RETRY_COUNT_HEADER), raised by one. The copy waits in the service's memory until the delay is over, so a process that stops before then loses it. A replay reads a copy only while it is still short of the end of the file.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn shipping(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(file, |b| { b // Three deliveries of one order, the first included; then the dead-letter key. .include(ship) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("orders.dead") .include(review) }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { shipping(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss")) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } src/main.rs fn shipping(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(file, |b| { b // Three deliveries of one order, the first included; then the dead-letter key. .include(subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Ship).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("orders.dead") .include(subscriber(FileStream::new("orders.dead"), Review).build()) }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { shipping(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss")) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts counts every delivery of one order, the first included. The third delivery is not retried: dead_letter appends it under orders.dead, payload and headers as they arrived. On a stream file the dead-letter key is one more stream key of the same file. A cap with no dead-letter key beside it writes the spent order nowhere.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders.dead"))] async fn review(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!( order.id, deliveries, "unpaid order needs a person to look at it" ); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Review; impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), Clients> for Review { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!( order.id, deliveries, "unpaid order needs a person to look at it" ); ready(Ok(())) } } review reads orders.dead like any other key. The retry-count header of a dead letter holds the number of deliveries the order got, 3 here. An operator who inspects the dead letters later reads them with a replay instead.

A stage's standard output reaches the next process and never its own input, so a copy cannot come back to the stage that deferred it. On StdioBroker the mount site names the key the copies go to, b.include(ship).out_retry(Publish).to("orders.retry"), and a later stage reads them (out_retry). The pipeline stage of Getting started is mounted this way. A stage that names no key does not start, because any handler may answer retry_after. The cap and the dead-letter key work on a pipe as they do on a file; a dead letter is a line under its key for a downstream stage.

The tests in the example file run the app in process on a paused clock, so tb.advance(RECHECK) lets the two seconds pass at once. One test clears the payment between two deliveries, and the order ships on the second. The dead-letter test runs both in process and on a real stream file with TestApp::start_live, where the delays pass on the real clock. Testing a file or pipeline service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, on an in-process transport or on a real stream file. The service under test is a checkout. An order arrives under orders, and the handler replies with a receipt under receipts. An order without an amount is dropped. An order over the fraud-check limit is held: the handler asks for it again in a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries an order goes to orders.review, the dead-letter key. The app is built by service(file), so a test chooses the file and main uses the production one. The service is the example file's own, examples/guide/testing.rs. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-sea-file in [dev-dependencies].

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; an_order_gets_a_receipt_in(tb).await } async fn an_order_gets_a_receipt_in(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .message(&Order { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { order: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; an_order_gets_a_receipt_in(tb).await } async fn an_order_gets_a_receipt_in(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .message(&Order { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { order: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects FileBroker to a log in memory. The path is never opened, so tests run side by side in one process. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<FileBroker>(). publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled and what reached receipts. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_without_an_amount_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .message(&Order { id: 2, amount_cents: 0, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_without_an_amount_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .message(&Order { id: 2, amount_cents: 0, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } settled checks the outcome the handler returned. assert_not_called checks that no receipt was appended.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn an_order_held_three_times_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let large = Order { id: 3, amount_cents: 250_000, }; tb.broker::<FileBroker>().message(&large).publish().await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The delay ends in a copy of the order, appended under `orders`. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Order>("orders") .assert_called(2) .with(&large) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "1"); // The third delivery is the last one: it is written under `orders.review` as it arrived. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<FileBroker>().subscriber("orders").outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .published::<Order>("orders.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&large); let large = Order { id: 3, amount_cents: 250_000, }; tb.broker::<FileBroker>().message(&large).publish().await?; tb.broker::<FileBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); The copy carries the retry count in a header, and published shows it under orders next to the test's own order. The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows, so the order goes to orders.review as it arrived. Each held delivery is recorded as Outcome::Nack.

documents.t: The in-process stream file is a log in memory, new for each broker value and shared by its clones. It keeps what a file keeps: Each stream key is numbered from one, and a live subscription starts at the tip. A replay reads what the log holds and completes at its end. Positions and seeks resolve against the log with the file's refusals. end_with_eos ends every subscription at shutdown. A log the service reads at startup is recorded on a clone of its broker before TestApp::start, as the Resuming and seeking tests do. The in-process pipe is standard input the test feeds and standard output the service writes. tb.broker::<StdioBroker>().message(..) is a line arriving under its key, and published::<T>(key) reads a line the stage wrote. A stage reads its own output only under loopback, as on a real pipe. Both transports refuse what the real ones refuse: a stream key the client does not take, an empty line on a pipe, a beacon interval that is not a multiple of 1024. The bytes of a .ss file, what a file keeps across runs, and the line format and the end of input on a real pipe show only on the real transport.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn an_order_gets_a_receipt_on_a_stream_file() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // A file of this run's own, so nothing an earlier run appended is read. let path = env::temp_dir().join(format!("checkout-{}.ss", process::id())); let file = FileBroker::new(path.to_string_lossy()); let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(file)).await?; an_order_gets_a_receipt_in(tb).await?; fs::remove_file(&path)?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn an_order_gets_a_receipt_on_a_stream_file() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // A file of this run's own, so nothing an earlier run appended is read. let path = env::temp_dir().join(format!("manual-checkout-{}.ss", process::id())); let file = FileBroker::new(path.to_string_lossy()); let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(file)).await?; an_order_gets_a_receipt_in(tb).await?; fs::remove_file(&path)?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start_live runs the same app on a real stream file in the temp directory. The transport is the local file system, so the live test needs no server and runs with the others in cargo test. The file is named after the process, so nothing an earlier run appended is read, and the test removes it at the end. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. A pipeline stage is tested live as a child process with piped standard input and output, as Shell pipelines shows.
